utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, you are to conclude your re-examination; 15 minute, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, it will be even less than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Less than 15 minutes, so much the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. I just have a few more questions to ask you. Yesterday, you made a reference in your testimony to collegium meetings. Can you tell us what these collegium meetings were, and how often they occurred?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were meetings of the corps command, or rather, the top officers in the corps command. In principle, they took place once a week; and, when necessary, either more frequently or less frequently, depending on the situation and the needs involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would the corps commander himself attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the commander was there, he did attend, or rather, he chaired the meetings of the collegium. If not, the meetings would be chaired by his deputy; that is to say, the Chief of Staff of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was invited, of course, I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you invited -- were you ordinarily invited, or did that occur only on special occasions?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often. Well, regularly, it would happen almost every time there was a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what level of commander was at the meeting; for example, were brigade commanders there, battalion commanders? How far down the chain of command did it go, in terms of participation at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Collegium meetings were attended by the members of the command; that is to say, the top officers in the corps command; and, when necessary, the commander could invite any commanding officer of any lower ranking units depending on the situation, depending on the subject that was to be discussed, that is. Also there were meetings that were attended by all commanders of brigades, but these were not meetings of the collegium. These were meetings, well, of the top officers at command level and brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how often did those meetings occur?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such meetings were held, depending on the situation, I cannot say exactly; that is to say, that such meetings did not have a previously set protocol and such meetings were not planned. It depended on the actual needs involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, you were asked in cross-examination some questions concerning the reports from the prosecutor's office, the military prosecutor's office that went into evidence. When a possible criminal violation was referred to the military prosecutor's office for investigation, can you tell us who would -- which body or which individuals would actually conduct the investigation on behalf of the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the answer to that question would be. That would belong to the line of work of the prosecutor's office, and the corps command did not have any kind of relationship of hierarchy with them, in terms of subordination. We just cooperated with them, but the military judiciary and the prosecutor's officer are independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you yourself participate in criminal investigations or conduct criminal investigations?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you -- do you recall receiving any complaints or protest letters from UNPROFOR about sniping and shelling of civilians?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the SRK command receiving them, and you being aware of them.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any of that. My line of work was completely independent of that. Not at a single point in time was I involved or my subordinates or was that the purview of my work in terms of relations with UNPROFOR, or rather, the relationship between the army of Republika Srpska and UNPROFOR. There were officer who is were in charge of UNPROFOR, and they indeed cooperated with the representatives of UNPROFOR. I wasn't one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have a few clarifying questions for you. The first question relates to your knowledge of the relation between the corps commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that is the accused, and General Ratko Mladic. Can you tell us, if you know, what was the operative relation between the two; and to be more specific, I'm asking you to tell us, if you know, what degree of freedom the accused had in conducting the military operations around Sarajevo at the time when you were working in the corps?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the relations were professional and soldierly, in terms of subordination; that is to say, the commander of the Main Staff was the superior of the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Perhaps I did not remember what the other part of your question was. Oh, freedom. The responsibilities of the corps commander are set, and it is specified which decisions he can take on his own and for which he has to seek the approval of his superior officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was exactly about the range of autonomy that the corps commander would have in deciding the military operations in and around Sarajevo at the time. Could you give us an example of an order coming from General Ratko Mladic and then being translated into action by the accused? What -- I'm curious about the degree of freedom which the accused had in determining the course of events.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really give you an answer, unless I were to engage in guesswork. I was never corps commander, so I don't know what the responsibilities of corps commanders are in terms of their work, in terms of holding that position, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But I suppose these questions would have been questions discussed during the collegium meetings, would they not?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for orders given by a superior, there is no discussion about that. You can only talk about how an order can best be carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If orders came from the supreme authority of General Mladic down to the corps, and the corps commander would then have to decide which actions were to be taken in -- in the fulfilment of the order that came from above, I suppose that during the collegium meetings the corps commander would inform the staff, the top staff, about the order that had come from above and just how he, the accused, would now implement these orders. So can you recall any such example from your participation in the collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure is fully regulated. There are regulations as to how an order is carried out and how a decision is made. It depends on the amount of freedom left to the subordinate officer by his superior in the order issued, so it has to do with the way in which subordinate units are to be used. Everything is regulated by the rules as to how decision are made. Members of the command can make proposals depending on the subject matter involved, or rather, the type of task that is to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'm not interested in the rules. I'm interested in knowing how did it apply in practice.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the corps worked in accordance with the rules; that is to say, how it was envisaged to make decisions. And the participation of assistant commanders and the Chief of Staff was there, according to the rules, in terms of the commander's decision. It also depended on the situation on the ground, how decisions would be made. Only the most important officers would be invited for a meeting or the entire command, if the situation made that possible. He made decisions on the basis of positions, or rather, proposals made by those officers who were either assistant commanders or the Chief of Staff, himself, so it depended on the proposals made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me put my question in a different way then. Did you ever, during your participation in the collegium meetings, hear the corps commander informing you about orders that you had received from the Supreme Command and the corps commanders decision as to how he would implement such orders? Did you ever witness that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the way things are done. It's customary; it's normal. There is not much dilemma there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. So my question was: Could you please explain to us or give an example of an order that had been received from the Supreme Command to the corps and how the corps commander then implemented those orders into practice?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that you are interested in the procedure itself. The corps commander, when he receives an order, presents that to the first meeting of the collegium that is held --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have already told you, Mr. Witness, that I'm not particularly interested in the what the rules said. I'm interested in hearing an example of an order that was given by General Mladic to the corps and knowing just how the accused implemented that order into practice; a concrete example. You have told us previously that you did witness such cases, and I would like you to explain to me an example of what happened.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you an example because I'm trying to explain how these things are done. As assistant commander for morale, I would get a task from the corps commander from the field of morale what kind of proposal -- or rather, in relation to this task what my proposal would be in terms of carrying out that task in the best possible way. That is the procedure involved. As for a concrete example, I cannot recall right now, only if...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's move on to something else. I would like to discuss with you something that you mentioned during examination-in-chief yesterday; the use of modified air bombs. And I think that you told us yesterday that you knew that such bombs were being used, and I think you also said that they were being used by your side as well as by the BiH side. Now, my question relates to your evaluation of the lawfulness of the use of such modified air bombs. You were in charge of legal affairs, among other things, and I suppose that the lawfulness of the use of such weapons is something that you would have discussed. So my first question is: What was your evaluation of the use of modified air bombs, of the lawfulness under international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view is that air bombs are a normal weapon in the air force. They had their exact purpose in terms of what they were being used for, so I believe that this type of weapon is permitted. I just know of air bombs that were used, because that was my own line of work at the beginning of my career. Specifically, I don't know -- I mean, I never saw this other way of using them, how these air bombs were used. I'm not aware of that, so I cannot tell you exactly whether it is permissible or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I realise that have you not seen it or expressed any opinion on it, but you -- I think you said that you had heard about such bombs being used in -- from the ground; that is to say, that they are being launched with rocket launchers in a modified way. That's why we call them modified air bombs. So you had heard about them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This description that you gave just now as to what this looks like is something that I first heard during my interview with the investigator; that is to say, on the 3rd of August last year. They actually told me what this was like. That was the first time I learned about this, from them, how these bombs are modified and how they were launched. I personally had never seen this weapon being used in that way, as in land launched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Given the fact that you were the chief of legal affairs in the corps, my question to you is whether you would have been consulted prior to the use of any such weapons? Let us assume that the question had arisen to use such weapon, and my question is would you then have been consulted about the lawfulness thereof?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I properly would not have been consulted on that because I'm not a legal man myself. I'm not a legal expert. I already explained that from a military point of view. The legal department belonged to my organ in terms of discipline, issuing orders, and so on. However, as for the professional side of lawyers' business, I could not interfere in that because I don't have proper qualifications for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that you yourself probably would not be consulted because you had no expertise in such matters. But your function, if I understand your position correctly, was to handle through the people working for you in your departments matters of -- of various questions, including legal questions. So if there were a question relating to the lawfulness of the use of a particular weapon, would that not have been discussed with someone in your department through you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, such a question was not raised at all, therefore, it was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, to follow up on this series of questions put to you by my colleague, I remember that yesterday you said that the army of the Republika Srpska, as well as the ABiH army on the Muslim side, had inherited the weapons of the JNA, the former Yugoslav army, and the weapons were located on both sides. And if I remember correctly, you mentioned the these air bombs as being part of these weapons.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So normally speaking, and according to your statement, one could well imagine that on the Serb side, as well as on the Muslim side, one could actually use such bombs or make use of such bombs. Now, you were the commander's assistant, and I'm talking about the commander of the SRK. According to you, what you thus inherited; namely, these air bombs, did you actually make use of these weapons? I'm putting the question to you as the assistant to the commander. Were you aware of the use of these weapons or not at all?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that I understood you well. The weapons that was at the disposal were being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Including the air bombs?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including air bombs; in other words, everything that could be used in combat and which was in the depots and storehouses in the area controlled by either warring party. It is only natural for them or us to use these weapons, because these were resources meant to be used for warfare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my last question. Can you confirm, as all the weapons were used, that these air bombs that you used were used solely by the air force, as you have just said; in other words, no modified air bombs were used.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the pre-war period? As far as I know, there were only air bombs that were dropped from aircraft. That's my knowledge. I don't know whether there were other types of bombs such as modified bombs. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I was about to dismiss the witness, but I see you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one or two questions which arise out of questions by the Bench. I don't know if you will permit me to ask them, but it's been the practice in other courtrooms when the Judges touch on areas and there are question that arise from that, the parties are permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us see, maybe it is the same thing that has been exercised in my mind, but let me hear from Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that would be an endless circle, and it would be contrary to the rules of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, not really, Mr. Tapuskovic, if you are also given a chance to clarify any matter that arises. If I give the Prosecutor a chance to ask questions arising out of the Judge's questioning, I would also afford you the same opportunity. So there would be no prejudice. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: First, I just want to see if I understood an answer that you gave, if I understood it correctly to the Judges' question. Is it your testimony that the first time you heard about modified air bombs, as opposed to air bombs, was in August of 2006?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was when I first was given a description of this type of weapon by the investigators. They described to me how it looked like, and it is true that I personally had never before seen this kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But had you before heard about this kind of weapon?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was a modified air bomb a weapon that was used by the SRK during the time that you were assistant commander for morale, religion, and legal affairs?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also during the interview with the investigator, I also heard for the first time that allegedly the radio television building had been targeted by a modified air bomb. That's what I was told on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With respect, I don't think that was an answer to the question. The question was: Was a modified air bomb a weapon that was used by the SRK during the time that you were assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't know specifically whether the SRK used these modified bombs. I suppose that there are documents showing this, and that it's something that can be found out. I personally never witnessed this kind of operation; therefore, I'm unable to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You say you never witnessed it. Did you ever hear about it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. Did --

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- an abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I really want to be precise here. Did you ever hear about modified air bombs being used by the SRK.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard this term "modified." What I heard was that air bombs were being used. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you heard about air bombs being used, how were they being used? Were they being launched from the ground, or were they being dropped by airplanes?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that during the interview with the investigators, I heard for the first time that they had been launched from the ground. I wasn't familiar with that kind of weapons or the mode of its use, and I still don't know anything about it. That's when I heard for the first time that this bomb was being launched from the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I'm not going to allow to you go any further because you're coming close to cross-examining your own witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think I'm just trying to get a clear answer to my question. I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe it is -- I believe it is sufficiently clear. What I'd like to find out is whether he had also heard of the same modified air bombs being used by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I had never heard this term "modified" until my interview with the investigators. All I have ever heard before was about air bombs and their usage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dragicevic, before you became the assistant commander for morale, religion, and legal affairs, and that happened on the 22nd of November, as we heard before, you were aware that both parties had modified air bombs at their disposal and that they had acquired them at the beginning of the war? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said as far as weapons and everything else was concerned, both parties had at their disposal what was available in the area under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also know that until you assumed your duties, and especially during the period where there was no no-fly zone imposed, that these bombs, air bombs were being used by both sides because they had aircrafts, they had helicopters, and things like that; and after that, a no-fly zone was imposed, especially on the Serbian side? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it was only natural for them to use them because this kind of weaponry was legitimate, and they used it depending on the type of targets they wished to engage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After the decision to impose a no-fly zone over Bosnia-Herzegovina WAS taken, and at least we can say that about the Serbian side, they were no longer able to use these air bombs that they had and kept for themselves after the departure of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, if planes are not flying, these bombs cannot be dropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of April and early May, when BiH army offensive was expected to be launched, we discussed yesterday the decision. Do you stand by it, that the decision was taken to give permission to use the weapons that the Serbian army -- Bosnian Serbian army had, could be used only after an attack began? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters didn't hear the answer that the witness gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the answer that you gave to that question, Colonel? The interpreter didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel, that concludes your testimony. We thank you for come together Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Edgerton will be handling the next witness. It's Mr. Karavelic. We will require a bit of a line change here on our team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I think Mr. Docherty would like to be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may be excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is not our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just before I begin, I wonder if Mr. Usher, when he has a moment, could have the tripod with the maps brought over to be beside the General. And while Mr. Usher is doing that, I'm able to deal with the statements, testimonies, and documents which were the subject of the Trial Chamber's order on 22nd February. Before I do that, could I just ask, sir, do you have your reading glasses with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us your name, please, and your present occupation.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: My name is Vahid Karavelic. Three years ago I retired. Up until then, I was a member of the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In these last three years, I have been engaged in different things, among other things, I work part-time for a company. I'm writing books, studying, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tells us at what rank you retired from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I retired with a rank of Major-General.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in preparation for your testimony here today, did you have an opportunity to review two of your statements to the Office of the Prosecutor; one dated November 2nd, 2001, and that's, for the record, ter number 03046, and the second dated 18 August 2006, and that's ter number 03047. General, did you have an opportunity to review these two statements in your own language?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you, following that review, have any additions, deletions, or other changes that you wish to make to shows statements?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: No, nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked at the time, would your testimony on those matters be the same as what is set out in those two statements?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the case, Your Honours, could I ask that the first statement dated 2nd November 2001, ter number 03046, be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P492, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then the second statement, as well, please, dated 18th August 2006, ter number 03047.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be P493, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, turning to two of your previous appearances before other Trial Chambers of this Tribunal, have you listened to your testimonies in the proceedings against General Galic and General Hadzihasanovic in your own language?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today during your testimony, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the case, then, Your Honours, could I ask the following be entered as the next exhibits. Again, pursuant to Your Honour's order of 22 February, ter number 03048 A to K; 03049 A to L; and 030350 A to K, those are the pages for the General' testimony in the Galic proceedings. If they could be entered as the next exhibit, Your Honour. And I would think that despite the fact they have separate ter numbers, they could be entered as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these will be admitted together at P494.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And with respect to the Hadzihasanovic testimony, the ter numbers are 03051 A to G; 03052 A; a 03053 A to F. If those could be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these will be admitted as P495.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Finally, as part of our tender and, again, pursuant to the order, I would like to ask about the associated exhibits referred to in the decision; ter number 02106, 02248, and 02777, all of which are dealt with in great detail in the statements and transcripts already exhibited. And in the Prosecution's appendix to our motion for their admission, we of course directed the Trial Chamber to the relevant pages of the statements and transcripts. Could I ask that they also be given exhibit numbers; and three separate, please. Those are three quite distinct documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just tell us what these are.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, and I can do that. I just have to make sure that I'm referring to the appropriate ter numbers, Your Honours. 02248 is a document dated 16 March 1995; an UNMO report on having heard a SRK officer say they will shoot women and children, and it was described a referred to by the witness in his statement dated 18 August 2006 at page 7. That's the first one. 2106 is a document dated 7 November 1994; a certified copy of a telegram from the VRS Main Staff from General Mladic instructing or forbidding any activities in connection with the blockade of UNPROFOR and confiscation of heavy weapons under their supervision, planning or conducting any offensive combat activities, and the use of weapons of bigger calibre on civilian targets in Sarajevo, forbidding these activities from being conducted without his express approval. And that's referred to in the witness' statement dated 18 August 2006 at page 3 of the English version. And 2777, the last one, is a map of Sarajevo that was prepared by the General and is described in his testimony in the Galic proceedings at page 11796 to 11806.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you just remind us of the evidential basis for the admission of these documents, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, these documents were already admitted by decision -- by the decision of 22nd February, and I have a copy of the decision available for Your Honours, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what are you seeking to do now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To have exhibit numbers assigned to each of these last three documents; no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I see. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right. I know it was a huge binder containing hundreds of documents, but now I understand what it is all about, that two or three documents are now being introduced from this whole bunch of documents, and it's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Tapuskovic gives his blessing, we can go ahead. Let's have them numbered --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honours. All I'm saying is that I understand what the Prosecutor is talking about. But I understand with the question that you asked is the relevance, and that's what I would like the Prosecutor to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, just -- she did give an explanation, and I believe that that certainly shows their relevance. Please have them numbered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 02106 becomes P496; 65 ter 02248 becomes P497; and 65 ter number 02777 becomes P498.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could move forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, in the 2001 statement, page 14, the last paragraph on page 14 and the first paragraph at the top of page 15 and page 16 of the Bosnian version, you refer to your relationship or the relationship with the MUP. In that paragraph, you explain the corps level procedure you would go through if circumstances called for MUP support to the 1st Corps. Now, would you, relating to that paragraph, would you or did you know anything about the composition of whatever unit you might receive from the MUP, what branches of the police service they might have been drawn from?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the civilian police were two separate entities. Speaking specifically about my own corps, it did cooperate with the civilian police in Sarajevo. When a unit would be received by way of assistance in certain situations, whenever I got support, assistance from the civilian police, I would always get a particular police unit, a unit as a unit. I was never interested and I did not know what the composition of that particular unit was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, if I can follow up with that answer, because I note you referred to civilian police, but, General, were there not several branches of the police forces in Sarajevo; the special police, the civilian police, the criminal police, and indeed your own military police?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: When I say "civilian police," I'm referring to the overall police force outside military structures.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So my -- my simple question then is: When you got a unit, do you know what branches of the police that unit might have come from, whether they might have come from the special police or the civilian police or any other arm of the police?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I have already given an answer to that. I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now during 1994 and 1995, do you recall how many times you were required to make this corps level special request for MUP support?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: That happened a few times. I cannot say exactly what the number was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was it something more than five, or less; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I think it was up to five.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall the circumstances, what those units might have been used for?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I recall a few particular sets of circumstances. I don't remember if I will be able to recall all. For instance, the circumstance of assisting in holding the defence line in front of Grbavica, in the centre of town; then when carrying out offensive combat action, at least once in 1994 and in 1995 at the southern outskirts of the town of Sarajevo, Igman, Bijeljina, and Treskavica, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the first instances you mentioned, holding the defence line in front of Grbavica, do you recall over what period of time that took place, how long that unit was on duty for?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact time. At any rate, it wasn't less than a few months, and I don't think it was more than a year.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And with respect to the instances, the single instance in 1994 and the instance in 1995, how long did you require MUP units for?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In these other situations, for as long as the combat task lasted; on average, it was ten, 15, to 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to go towards your Galic testimony, you said at page 1178 that reserve police were never used as combatants. Now, in relation to the use of police as combatants by officers of your corps, I wonder if I could ask for Exhibit D61, which has been marked for identification, to be brought up on the screen. General, do you see a document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document in the first paragraph refers to agreement of 2 July 1995 between the Main Staff commander and the Minister of the Internal Affairs aimed at the defence of the town of Sarajevo, and talks specifically in -- of the engagement of MUP units in paragraph 1. Is this document accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the agreement that the document refers to?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I remember these agreements, and I was involved in it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what exactly the agreement was, General?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Well, the result of that agreement was that during the course of 1992 and 1993, particularly in the beginning --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, General. I was referring to the agreement that this document refers to, 2nd July 1995.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The aim of this agreement was exclusively to simplify the use of units; that is to say, police from police stations, from local level, from municipal level, that is, for the needs of the brigades of my corps. That is why this agreement was made, and it has to do with the following. If there is a crisis and if the defence line is under threat in the case of a particular brigade, then this order and agreement would make it possible for the commander of that same brigade to turn to the head of the police administration in that municipality and that a number of policemen from that municipality would come to assist the threatened defence line. I would like to point out that this could be done without carrying out the entire procedure. The entire procedure, if I can talk about that now, would mean that the brigade commander would have to ask his own division commander to give him authority to use the police. He'd ask me in turn and I would have to ask the army commander and then they would have to ask the Supreme Command and then the Supreme Command would have to order that to the Minister of the Interior and then the Minister of the Interior would have to work done his own chain so that this local police could help the brigade on the defence line. The aim of this agreement was to avoid that long chain.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just with respect to this agreement, did that, General, pertain to the use of police in combat or in defence?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In defence. And that's what it says here; defence only.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, moving on to another area, General, in your position as corps commander, could you tell us what information you would receive about opposing forces?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I received different kinds of information. But in my work, I relied on receiving information from our official legal services; that is to say, from our official organs. I received information from two directions: Information upwards, in terms of my own chain of command, and I received information from services and organs of my superior command. I would receive information certainly about overall activities of the aggressor forces, about their movements, about their intentions, about what they did, about their armaments and equipment, about their deployment, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, did you also receive information about the targeting of civilians on Bosnian-held territory, the targeting of civilians by sniping?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did receive information of that type as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would those reports and -- would you have received information about the location of the origin of fire sniper shots?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I can just clarify one thing. For the greater part of the war your command headquarters was in fact in the city of Sarajevo as well. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in paragraph 11 of your 2001 statement, and paragraph 42 of your 2006 statement, you talk about where snipers were stationed. Is that information on the basis of both reports that you received from your staff and military organs and your own personal observations and experiences?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you refer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object. I think that these are leading questions, but it is for you to judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Had you asked first, Ms. Edgerton, about the reports that he received from his staff and military organs, you had not asked about that first. Well, you should have. So in future, please ensure no leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour, and apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you have to do more than your best. It's just not permissible. The evidence is, in fact, valueless when you lead, because it means that it is coming from you, not from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, you refer in your statement to some permanent sniper positions. Could you tell the Trial Chamber which positions you're referring to when you describe those?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Of course, I can. We used this jargon, "sniper, sniper, sniper," but it's not only snipers that were killing in Sarajevo. Many other weapons in addition to snipers can also target as precisely as snipers, but snipers are invariably mentioned. And there were these locations that throughout the war were there constantly located in terms of these points from where the population of the city was being killed all the time. I can refer to a few of them, although they did exist throughout the defence line in the town of Sarajevo. A boarder location is -- from which there was a lot of targeting was the area of Debelo Brdo, or rather, the Jewish cemetery, as one area. Another location is the curve of a road, the road between Lukavica and Pale above Skenderija, precisely above Debelo Brdo. The next location is the broader area of Grdonje, or Spicasta Stijena; then the location at Grbavica, the four sky-scrapers that were a source of danger throughout the war for the town of Sarajevo...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should explain for the benefit of the record that we broke earlier because of the technical problem, but that has been fixed and you're now ready to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I go further I see that I omitted to -- with respect to the Exhibit D61, it was previously marked for identification, and I omitted to have it tendered now that the witness has spoken to it. I would ask it no longer be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Precisely, yes. It will keep the MFI number without the MFI.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that then will become D61.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, when we broke, we were discussing -- you had identified a number of permanent sniper locations by name, and if I could ask you a couple of things with respect to the locations you mentioned, Debelo Brdo; the curve of the road between Lukavica and Pale, above Skenderija; the border area of Grdonj on Spicasta Stijena; four sky-scrapers at Grbavica. Were all of these locations on -- were these locations on Bosnian-held territory or Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Territory that was under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the area of Debelo Brdo, the Jewish cemetery, and the curve of the road, were there areas of Bosnian-held territory particularly vulnerable to sniper fire from those locations?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, because those locations are very close to the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And with respect to the area of Grdonj and Spicasta Stijena, were there areas of Bosnian-held territory which were particularly vulnerable from that location?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Those areas were not under the control of the my corps. They were under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as well, except that is on the other side of town. That point was also very close to the centre of town; and from that point, one could observe and cover, if I can put it that way, almost all of the municipality of Stari Grad and the municipality of Centar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, finally, with respect to the four sky-scrapers at Grbavica, were there areas of Bosnian-held territory which were vulnerable to sniper fire from those locations?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: As for these four sky-scrapers, they were also under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, on the left bank of the Miljacka river, on Grbavica. Actually, from there a large part of the centre of the town, Sarajevo was covered from there; that is to say, from those four sky-scrapers. And in that way one could cut across town itself from the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina or from the Marshal Tito barracks or the museum, all of that is the broader area; and then to the east and then to the west, all the way to Cengic Vila.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I could ask you, General, to turn to map on the left-hand side beside you and perhaps have the camera focus on that map, and for the record that map bears the ter number 02927. Could you just point out on the map, please, the area that you were referring to as the Debelo Brdo-Jewish cemetery area when you described a permanent sniper location?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The area of Debelo Brdo and the Jewish cemetery is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The area of the curve of the road --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the accused, Dragomir Milosevic, would have to be able to see what the witness is pointing at. He cannot see the map. He absolutely cannot see the locations pointed out by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, can we have the map turned in such a way as to enable the accused to see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could assist, if the accused looks at his e-court monitor, he should be able to see a blow-up portion of the map that the witness has just pointed it now. It's been magnified to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear that? Mr. Milosevic, did you hear that? If you look, Mr. Milosevic. Yes, please look at the e-court map, which has been magnified.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the record, the magnification that appears on the screen bears the ter number 02927C.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, you had almost pointed out, as far as I could see, the location of the curve on the road to Pale. Could you show us that again?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The other area, the other location is precisely this curve above town, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, if I could ask you to turn to the screen, the monitor in front of you, the computer monitor in front of you, this -- could you tell the Trial Chamber whether or not you see the confrontation lines represented on this map?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, over the course of your tour of duty as corps commander, did you -- were you familiar with the perimeter of the confrontation line around Sarajevo? Did you become familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you're familiar with this particular location as depicted?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I was familiar with many locations, not to say all of them, but this one in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, is the front line as it's represented on this map, to the best of your recollection, accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, one might say that it's accurate. However, in several locations and points, there are certain points actually that are not depicted properly on the defence line; in other words, they are shown incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, could I then invite you to take the electronic marking tool from the monitor to the right of you and make the corrections on the map in front of you to reflect what you understood the front lines to be in 1994/1995.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Specifically, here at Debelo Brdo, this blue line runs directly through Debelo Brdo which makes it appear that practically my corps held the peak of Debelo Brdo, which is not true. This line should approximately go like this, as I just drew it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For the record, then, the witness has made a bright blue line, which he has indicated reflects -- accurately reflects the confrontation line in 1994/1995 at the location of Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are there any other corrections you wish to make on the front line as depicted on this map, then, General?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: When I looked at this map, I noticed a couple of places; specifically, Spicasta Stijena and Grdonj.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the case, with respect to this particular image then, could I ask 02927C be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P499, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As the General has mentioned Spicasta Stijena, perhaps we could have a further image on the monitor, 02927B.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps, while we're waiting, General, I could ask you the following question: Could you tell us what the situation was on Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The situation at Spicasta Stijena was approximately the following: Since the beginning, until the end of the war, Spicasta Stijena was being held by the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. From the outset of the war, until the last day of the war, they saw death over the city of Sarajevo from Spicasta Stijena from various kinds of weapons. It is a dominant point above the entire out town and the municipality of Centar. It is an excellent vantage point and offers a perfect view of the area. There is a densely populated area immediately below Spicasta Stijena; and in front of it, there's a vertical stone wall which provided a very solid defence because it's very difficult to access it from the front side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, General. If I could stop you there and ask you to look at the image on the monitor in front of you. You've just spoken of a vertical stone wall. Do you see the area on -- first of all, could you indicate for the Trial Chamber the elevation of Spicasta Stijena, if you see it on the map in front of you.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: You mean with respect to the first neighbourhood next to it or what? The elevation is 895 metres. It's a TT point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to the peak of the elevation, please.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: This triangle which I marked with a red dot is the elevation point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you please put a small number 1 beside that.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated the presence of a stone wall which provided a very solid defence. Could you indicate -- are you able to indicate the area where the stone wall was?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Precisely to the south, below this red point, you can see a very many contours close to one another. Between this red line and the blue line there are many contours which indicates that it's a very sharp, steep terrain, almost vertical.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us the approximate distance between the elevation of Spicasta Stijena and Grdonj?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The map shows this clearly. It's between 300 and 500 metres. Let's say no more than 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you -- no more than 500 metres in which direction, please?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Towards east.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the front line as it's represented here on this map, is that, to the best of your recollection, accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: It's somewhat different, what I can see in this map, and if I may draw ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. While we're waiting for the witness's clarification, I think the witness said that Grdonj would be 500 metres to the east of Spicasta Stijena. On my map at least I have it south-west. Could you please ask the witness to clarify whether the indication is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, you have indeed indicated that Grdonj lay between 300 and 500 metres to the east of Spicasta Stijena. Now if this map is properly oriented did Grdonj lie indeed to the east or to the west of Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I understood the question properly, and that is where Spicasta Stijena was with respect to Grdonj. With respect to Grdonj, Spicasta Stijena is to the east, or more precisely, north-easterly direction, 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, obviously something is unclear here and needs to be clarified. We need to specify these elevation of Grdonj and the height of Spicasta Stijena. As far as I can see, Grdonj is indeed to the east from Spicasta Stijena. If one reads a map and we need to clarify this. Grdonj 906 metres at Spicasta; Stijena 895 metres; and Grdonj is to the east of Spicasta Stijena. It cannot be to the west at all. If you take a look, I'm not an expert, but that much I can understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the Witness was abundantly clear when he finally specified that with respect to Grdonj, Spicasta Stijena is in a north-easterly direction 500 metres and if my learned friend is asking a question of the witness to specify what the various elevations of these heights are, according to meters I would suggest that might be a question he can nut his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes that is always open to Mr. Tapuskovic. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record the witness has drawn a blue line indicating accurately the -- in his submission the confrontation line and where it lies between 1994 and 1995. I would ask that that be tendered or marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 02927B, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that becomes Exhibit P500.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, witness --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: And the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps forces were deployed in a different way, not as the map is showing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps then if the P500 could remain on the screen and he could -- the witness could, since he wishes to make a correction, correct P500 we could then have it marked as a further exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, for the record, with a red line the witness has marked the accurate disposition, in his view, of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps forces at Spicasta Stijena. Perhaps I could ask that be marked as P501.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- oh.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if possible, we can just keep all of these markings together as P500.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. I didn't realise that was possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, if I could ask you to just turn back to the map on the board in behind you and look generally at the front line as it's depicted on this map. Generally speaking, with the exceptions of the corrections that you have indicated, is this front line, does it accurately represent the front line as you understood it to be in 1994 and 1995, again, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, generally speaking. But in certain aspects, it's not very accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What would those aspects be, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I can give you other deviations and mistakes that I myself detected because this map was made by staff officers who did it in haste and didn't care too much about accuracy. This kind of map needs to be done with very thin felt-point pens. I can give you further examples of the mistakes that I noticed, although I myself don't know everything either.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you describe to us some deviations you wish to clarify, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He should tell us where he is pointing to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: One of the deviations is in the eastern parts. This is not where my lines were. They were not so much forward. They were more to the backward -- to 100 to 200 metres backward. I'm talking about this area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, can I, just for the record, indicate that the witness is referring to the confrontation line which lies, as the map goes, to the east of the designation "152 Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please go on, sir.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Next in the north-west part where I'm pointing now, in this area as well, my lines were not so much forward. They were also more to the back by 100 to 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has pointed to the area of Rajlovac and indicated the line should be redrawn roughly across lettering that reads "3-BB" to the east of Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, sir, I note that this map indicates some placement or disposition of armament within the area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. May I just ask the witness whether there was any particular reason why his line was not more forward in that particular area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Due to poorly qualified and incompetent officers who did this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't mean the actual drawing. What you have said is that your line was not where it is indicated on the map but some 200 to 300 metres back. And I wanted to find out if there was a particular reason why your line was where it actually was. In particular, was there any military reason why your line was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood the question correctly, here, in the western, or rather, eastern part of the city of Sarajevo, huge area are clear -- or there are huge clearings and I had to withdraw into the depth in order to be on the rear ridge and be protected and camouflaged as much as possible. That was the only way to survive and sustain in these places. In this area here, the line has gone too much into the plain or the valley. This flat terrain does not offer good opportunity for fighting against the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I had to adhere to natural features that were helpful in my defence. That is why it was more logical to have the line on the slopes. And from this point on, the terrain is going upwards or ascending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, sir, I note on this map there is some -- this maps denotes some disposition of weapons throughout the inner area of Sarajevo. You have already indicated that this map was prepared by officers of your division. So perhaps you're in a position to answer this. Are you aware, sir, how long the disposition of armament in a map like this would be effective for?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I can speak in general terms. No disposition of armament inside the city of Sarajevo did -- should not have been longer in terms of its remaining on a certain firing position and that involves seven, eight, maximum 15 days. Sometimes positions -- firing positions had to be changed many times in a single day. It all depended on when it is going to be spotted. Once it is spotted, it has to be shifted; otherwise, this firing position have been destroyed by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask that the map now receive an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, will be P501.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the record, that is ter number 02927.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, we were speaking originally about sniping, and perhaps for a brief period of time we could go back to that subject. Based on your experience in Sarajevo, do you have an opinion as to the level of skill or professionalism of snipers or sharpshooters under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: All I can say is this: During the war, or rather, in 1993, 1994, and 1995, there was information and I received reports, and it -- I think it can be found in many a report, and that was obvious the case that special units and special groups of this or that sort used to come to take part in attacks on Sarajevo. They most -- in most cases, they came to Grbavica and were billeted in the general area of Grbavica. Those special units were well armed, well equipped, and well trained. There was a huge number of such reports. What I actually felt and experienced I can say that I had been through a lot, but I cannot confirm whether this was the result of the operation of these units specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. If I could go back to the original question. I asked you about snipers or sharpshooters under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and your answer referred to special units. So perhaps I could ask you now, two follow-up questions. Do you have an opinion as to whether these special units were under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That's the first question; and secondly could we go back to the original question to talk about the level of skill and professionalism of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps snipers generally.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of the fact whether these units were part of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, an inherent part, and even if they weren't they had to be incorporated into the chain of command of the SRK. When you have such units coming to the area it goes without saying that they are excellently trained and prepared for waging a war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Perhaps we'll move on now. At page 12 of your statement in 2001, you referred to four main VRS artillery positions which could reach any part of town. Could you give us the names of the locations you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The eastern part of town -- that is the general area of Hresa and Borije, that's one area. To the north of the town -- the northern area, was in Paljevac, and this map doesn't show this particular area. But anyway, it refers to this general area that I'm just pointing with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I'm sorry. General, we didn't get the name of the area, the second area you were naming.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was it Paljevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paljevac, and there is a hill also.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. You have named two location and in your statement you refer to four main VRS artillery positions?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: THE INTERPRETER: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember the other two you were thinking of when you identified those four locations. Could you name the other two, please?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: A third location is to the south -- no, excuse me, to the west, or rather, north-west. And that's the area of Paljevo, all the way to Hrasnica, and this area is here. And a fourth location is to the south of the city of Sarajevo. That's the area of Toplik; this one that I'm pointing now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Usher, would be able to remove this map and I'll ask the General to have a look at the map underneath and meanwhile, if I could ask Mr. Registrar to call up image 02789C.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, perhaps this will make it easier for you. Could you turn to the map that appears on the tripod behind you and tell us whether you recognise or are able to tell us what this type of map is.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: It's a topographic map in which the plan of operation of the artillery of the SRK is being entered, or, rather its corps artillery group as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you to tell us whether you see those four locations you have spoken about on this map that would be helpful. And in fact, general, if you should turn to the monitor in front of you and you should be seeing a close-up image from that map, and that might make it easier for you and everyone in the court to see. Do you see the locations that you were referring to on the image on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The first location that I mentioned is precisely -- shall I put a circle?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, please, if you see it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The first location that I mentioned is Hresa and Borije, and it's here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you mark that first location with a number 1, please.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The second location, is in the area of Blagovac, which is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you mark that with a number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The third location is the area of Paljevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Area of Paljevo is, for the record marked with a number 3.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: And the fourth location is Toplik . That is the area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Marked with the number 4. Now, General, could I ask you, over the course of your military training did you receive any training in reading and understanding maps like these?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you receive training in making maps like these?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then, General, are you able to explain to us what the markings of squares are which appear scattered through the city of Sarajevo on this map?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: These small scares, or rather, rectangles denote the targets that are planned for the purpose of this artillery that I marked with number 1, in terms of the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us perhaps what size of area those targets purport to cover?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Most often, when such rectangles are placed, they denote an area of 100 by 100 metres or 100 by 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this marked as an exhibit, please, 02789C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P502, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, then, General, with regard to such maps and the notation of targets on these maps, what are we to understand as to target selection? Are targets for an operation determined usually in advance?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could also ask for the larger map, 02789, to be marked as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes P503.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just if I could ask one further question with respect to the text you see, General, on the image on the screen in front you beside number 1, could you tell us what that text reads? Are you able to read it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could it possibly be enlarged, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What does it say, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: What is says here in this one circle that denoted an artillery firing position that in this firing position of Gnjilo Brdo, there is a Howitzer of 122 millimetres, four pieces, then a squat of 150 millimetre weaponry, one weapon. And the two pieces in terms of Howitzers of 122 millimetres were attached at Ponor in some other place, and it would probably be returned subsequently, so there would be a total of six 122 millimetre Howitzers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder, Mr. Usher, if could you remove this map so that the General can see the map below that. And, Mr. Registrar, you could put the cutout 02788B on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, could you turn to the map in behind you and tell us, explain to us what this map is?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: The interpreter cannot hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This map shows planned targets for artillery fire, different types of artillery fire, of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. In this part here against the town of Sarajevo and in this area --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General. Could you tell us what you're pointing at, please, when you say "this part here."

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: This area that I'm indicating now includes three firing positions like in the previous brief map. That is the boarder area of Hresa and Borije to the east of Sarajevo. And in this case, the planned targets are --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Excuse me. For the record, the witness indicated a larger circle on the map to the east of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: From these firing positions, from Hresa and Borije to the east of Sarajevo, fire was planned, or rather, targets for that artillery that was to target the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, could I ask you if you see a name on the top left-hand corner of the map in front of you, top left-hand corner. Can you read the name?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. "I approve commander, Major-General Stanislav Galic," and there is a signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will have to object to this. We are dealing with the period of time between the 10th of August and -- the 10th of August, 1994 and the 21st of November, 1995. So I think it would be appropriate if that were to be discussed first, whether all these maps date back to the time when Galic was commander. I think that as for the period of time that we are dealing with, these maps are not relevant. It is for you to assess whether we can deal with that anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the period of time that you're dealing with, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, by asking one further question of the witness, I can assist with respect to the relevance of these maps and more particularly the locations he's identified as being mortar -- sorry, firing positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what about the time-period, that will also be clarified?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
