utterances.text: By asking the witness whose name appeared on that, I was hoping that I was making the time-period within which we were talking about quite obvious. This is a map dating from a period of time of the tenure of the accused's predecessor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you're going to ask a question now which will demonstrate the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I hope so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, you've talked and given us detail about four main VRS artillery positions, which you originally referred to in your 2001 statement; in particular, one called Hresa Borije, which you have identified on the map in front of you. Can you turn to the image that appears on the screen in front of you as well. Do you see Hresa Borije on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you indicate Hresa Borije.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indicating with a circle, for the record, the location of the area of Hresa Borije.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, to the best of your recollection, was the firing position that you've described in your statement -- were the firing positions that you've described in your statement, as the four artillery positions, were they permanent, or were they -- did they change? Did they move?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: For me, they were permanent in the area of Hresa Borije. Now, whether they had several different shelters and moved from time to time from one position to another, due to my occasional shelling, that is a different matter. But as far as I was concerned, they were permanent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say "permanent," what time-period do you mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I mean the time-period -- well, at any rate, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps could have a much longer period of time than me. They could have been there for a month or even more than that. And then if there was no fire coming from me, they could hold out for a year, perhaps even longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand, sir. When you say "permanent," how long a period of time do you mean in the case of this firing position?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In this case, when speaking of this firing position, at any the rate, it is longer. They would probably have a few months or perhaps a year or even more than a year at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember firing as coming from this position in the period prior to 1994?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Prior to and afterwards as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say "afterwards," do you recall firing coming from this position up until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, having asked those questions, could I ask -- could I submit this as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit P504.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could I ask the map itself, the larger map, ter number 2788, be given a further exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be P505.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Usher, there is one further map for the General.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, sir, we're going to move next to the subject of modified air bombs which you deal with at paragraphs 32 to 35 of your 2006 statement. And let me begin by asking you this: Sir, to your knowledge, did the 1st Corps have anything like or as powerful or of the same calibre as modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did the 1st Corps have any modified air bombs, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could you turn to the map behind you, which bears the number 02792, and tell us whether you understand, based on your experience, what this map depicts?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: "A decision of the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps for offensive combat activities." That is what is written on the map, under the name of "Lukavac 95."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you see a name written on the tap left-hand corner of the map?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: It says, "I approve commander, Colonel General Ratko Mladic." On his behalf, it was Milovanovic who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you see a name on the bottom right-hand corner of the map.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: It says, "commander, Major-General Dragomir Milosevic," with a signature and stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, sir, have you, in the course of your military training and activity, received training in the reading of maps, operational maps which were used to plan combat activities?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is this such a map?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And perhaps I could ask, then, Mr. Registrar, if the ter number 02792A could be called up, and we may have a translation available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Edgerton, just a minute, please. Witness, according to some testimonies, the weapons used by the various armies, whether it be the Republika Srpska army or the ABiH army, of the Muslims, the weapons, generally speaking, were inherited from the former JNA. According to you, on the Muslim side were there any air bombs that could have been used on board military aircraft or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, are you insulting me when you are telling me Muslim army when you say Muslim army. Secondly, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have air bombs. I assert with full responsibility that in the area of responsibility of my corps there never were any or were they ever used or anything even similar to it. Viewing other types of armaments as a whole, it is absolutely correct that in terms of what we had which was minimal, most of those weapons were of the same provenance like the weapons of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, perhaps I could just ask you to make a further precision significance reading this question and the answer. I had indicated to you we were going to discuss the subject of modified air bombs, and I stress the word "modified." And the question from His Honour Judge Mindua, referred to air bombs without the prefix "modified." Now in your response, you said the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have air bombs. Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He said in his corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, page 24, line 3 he says the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have air bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And then he goes on to say I assert with full responsibility that in the area of responsibility of my corps there were -- there never were any or were they ever used or anything even similar to it. So I take it he is saying -- he is confining himself to his corps. Perhaps you would like to have him clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to find that out, Your Honour, and to understand if he is referring to air bombs or modified air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, did you understand the comments and my response to Judge Robinson. First of all, in your answer are you confining yourself to assets held only by the 1st Corps, or are you discussing the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? That's the first question.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: For me, it's all the same, whether some type of original air bomb was there or a modified air bomb. I put that within the context of a single concept. As far as I know, it's army of Bosnia and Herzegovina never had any such thing at their disposal. Therefore, my corps did not have any such thing at its disposal or did it ever use such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if I understand your assertion, your assertion is your corps did not have modified air bombs nor did they have air bombs which could be dropped from an aeroplane. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the same thing applies to the ABiH army as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, then, how far do you know? You say as far as you know. That seems to suggest that there may be some uncertainty on your part. Please clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that the fact that I was corps commander practically throughout the war in the biggest corps in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that, is telling enough, and I proceed from the notion that there is not a single person who knows everything. So that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Right. So you -- you do allow, then, for the possibility that some other corps in the ABiH army might have had modified air bombs and you might not have known of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know with certainty whether I was born on that date that is indicated in my ID. Perhaps somebody made a mistake and wrote down a different date. But I claim from my position that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go back or go now to the image that is on the screen in front of you which is you see, General which is a magnification of the legend that appears on the bottom left-hand corner of this map. Could you read to us -- sorry, before I ask you that question, perhaps you could explain this legend and what information generally it sets out.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The legend says on top: The balance of forces where the offensive activities take place of our forces and the enemy forces. When it says "our forces" here, that is the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and the enemy is the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This legend is split in half. The left half speaks of the number of persons and all types of weapons available to that part of the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that is going to carry out offensive activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect -- General, with respect to the list of weapons that appears on that legend, if I could take you down to item number 10, I think, in the list of weapons.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It says here "launcher AB." I think it means "lanser aviobomba"; that is to say, launcher of airbombs, total 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if you could go to the other side of the legend to the corresponding entry where it says "launcher of aerial bombs available to the enemy forces," what does it say?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Here is says "launcher of air bombs" and then there is just a hyphen, that means zero, nothing. There aren't any.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask that this cutout be marked as the next exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes P506.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the larger map as well, ter 02972.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P507.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, I would like you to look at a series of documents in secession, that means one after the other, that I'm going to have asked to be called on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The first one, Mr. Registrar, bears the number 02414.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I don't have a document with that 65 ter number 02414.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, and perhaps my colleague, Ms. Bosnjakovic, can assist. I have hard copies available. I will offer them up to go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please have it placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find the picture of what should be going out on the ELMO on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, do you see the document dated 8 June 1995 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in this document, an artillery commander is requesting information on a number of items. Could you tell us what the first item is he is requesting information on?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The first item that information is being sought for is the number of air bomb launchers according to the types, depending on what they're capable of launching.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And does this document set out pursuant to whose order this request is being made?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Based on the order of the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, it was actually drafted by his head of artillery, Colonel Tadija Manojlovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could ask that this receive the next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes P508.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The next document, which, I believe, Mr. Registrar, will be electronically available, bears the ter number 02419.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, do you see a response from the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what does it say with respect to air bomb launchers?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: This report confirms that air bomb launcher is available, one piece for 105 and 205 kilos, monorail - and if you can move it a little bit the, I can't see the end of the sentence - monorail called Koseva.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could ask this be given the next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P509.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn to a further document, which according to my records bears the number 02422, but it doesn't appear that it sits in e-court so I have hard copies available again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, do you see -- General, do you see a response from the 1st Romania Brigade on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what does it say with respect to air bomb launchers?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In this document, the command of the 1st Romania Brigade informs the command of the SRK that they don't have an air bomb launcher but that one is being currently manufactured.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could ask that be marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P510, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The next document I'd like to refer to is -- bears the number 02428, and it should be available electronically.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, this further response from the Ilidza Brigade, do you see it on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What does it say with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the question that is troubling us is whether these documents can properly be admitted through this witness. All he is doing is merely confirming what you have read to him to be in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps then, Your Honour, there are two more documents, and one question at the end of that may assist Your Honours in making a determination as do whether they are properly admitted through this witness. I'll proceed through the documents without offering each one at the conclusion of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you should just ask the question now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Hmm, with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It may save us time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It may save us time, but it may not give us all the answers, Your Honours and I'm ending the end of my examination-in-chief very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll follow you this time, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for the indulgence, Your Honour. If I can have further indulgence because I need to consult the transcript for a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, do you know Colonel Vladimir Radojicic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I don't know him but I have heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who did you know him to be?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: According to this, he was the commander of the 1st Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, sir, can you see what Colonel Radojicic confirms with respect to an air bomb launcher in item number 1 on this document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Under item number 1, he confirmed to be in position of one -- possession of one air bomb launcher which can launch 100 and 250 kilo air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And one final document, please, if I may. It bears the number 2432, and it should be available electronically.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, can you look at the document that appears in front of you. A response from Commander Josipovic in relation to the first document. And what does he confirm as to whether or not his brigade has an air bomb launcher?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: This document also shows that the commander of the 3rd Brigade is confirming to be in possession of an air bomb launcher, in brackets, 100, 200, and 250 kilos, one piece.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, General, now you have looked at a number of documents from various SRK brigades speaking about whether they have air bomb launchers in their possession. How does the total number of air bomb launchers correspond with the number of air bomb launchers set out in the map you looked at earlier?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I think that these reports show that there were even more of them than the number shown in the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which map we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For my friend's benefit, that would be the map that appears on the tripod to the witness's left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Has that been admitted; if so, what is the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The larger map hasn't yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The larger map has not yet been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The cutout, the electronic image, the cutout of the legend has been admitted, and I omitted to tender the map as a whole, which I should. The cutout bears the number 504.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: P505 was the larger map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I stand corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the map has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it the cutout that is the relevant part?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For the Prosecution's case, the cutout is the most -- the most significant part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, very well. Did you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At page 32, lines 16 and 17, the witness said: "I think that these reports show that there were even more of them than the number shown on the map." And that being the case, Your Honour, I would now like to ask the following documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness didn't show at all anything in relation to air bombs. I don't actually know what he showed us in the map. He didn't show anything. What he did show on the map was that there were no launchers for air bombs. There were two air bombs; but in the other box, he said there were no launchers. That's what he has shown, nothing else. The map shows that there were no launchers. That's what he said a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I can clarify any unclarity with one question, Your Honour, to the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, if you can turn to the legend on the map in front of you, on the right-hand side of the legend, where it sets out weaponry available to enemy forces, and you have already given evidence that there are no air bombs listed. Is that consistent with your information as to whether any air bombs were in possession of the ABiH 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. When they were preparing the offensive operation, they had accurate assessment. When they said that they themselves had two launchers, they did not put any number and left this box blank when it concerned my forces. In other words, they had two pieces and I had zero pieces, so their assessment was accurate, and they knew that I didn't have any air bomb launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I truly have to object to this. I don't see that these positions of launchers are plotted anywhere in the map, nor did the witness show us anything in relation to the use of the launchers in this particular instances, except for what he just repeated now. I don't understand, and I think that this needs to be clarified for the benefit of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, have you extracted from the witness any evidence as to the number of air bombs specified anywhere on the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The witness was not asked whether he was able to see indications on that map that would denote air bombs. He was asked about whether he could recognise the symbols that denote any other -- other large artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The point is when you asked him about correspondence between something on the map and something in the document --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I didn't ask him about the correspondence with anything on the map. I asked him about the legend. We did not discuss any items on the map whatsoever. We only discussed the information contained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's what I meant. I was speaking of the legend as being part of the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is there in the legend that indicates a number? That's what I'm not clear about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have, Mr. Registrar, 02788B back on the screen, please. My apologies, 02792A, and my apologies to the Chamber for being numerically deficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, do you see the legend to the map that's beside you on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, tell us, General, if you do where, then, on this legend it indicates the number of air bomb launchers available to -- and I believe the translation would be "our forces."

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In the left-hand half of this legend, it refers to the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps intended for these offensive operations. And under item 10, among other things, they will have at their disposal two pieces of air bomb launchers. In the right-hand side of the -- half of the legend, which refers to my forces as enemy forces, this same item shows the quantity of launchers as zero or hyphen, that is based on their assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does that clarify matters for Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to take the break. We'll take the break, and when we return I will hear arguments from both sides as to whether these documents should be admitted or whether they should not be marked for identification. That's P508, 509, 510, 511. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I'll hear you as to why these documents should be admitted through this witness instead of become marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in that regard, and I've looked at these documents in some detail over the break, they're signed; they're stamped; they, on their face, on their very face have the appearance of authenticity. They're directly relevant, Your Honours, because they deal specifically with the air bombs, which the witness has shown some knowledge of. The air bombs in the period in 1995, in the period covered by the map, which the witness dealt with the legend of; and probably most significantly, Your Honour, my submission would be there was no objection from Defence counsel as to the admission of any of these documents until the moment it was raised by Your Honours. So in light of all those, Your Honours, my submission would be they could be admitted as exhibits at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, would that be consistent with the practice that we have been following as to the admission of documents in the trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think very much so, Your Honour. I'm of the view, and Mr. Whiting has confirmed, that the Prosecution has throughout the course of this trial agreed to the admission of documents which would normally be marked for identification. So I think admitting these documents now would he very much in line with the practice that has been followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Prosecution has agreed to the admission of documents. These are documents tendered by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Edgerton has asked me to address this, since it's a matter with the trial. I believe that we have agreed on certain occasions, and I say this based on my memory. I can't give you an example and I cannot say with 100 per cent certainty about this, but I believe we have agreed at times to the admission of documents into evidence, even though we could have made the objection that they shouldn't only be admitted for identification. And it seems to me that where the Defence has not made any objection to their admission into evidence that they should come into evidence and not simply be marked for identification. I think that I is a sufficient basis for their admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is true on several occasions the Prosecutor agreed with certain proposals by the Defence for the documents to be marked for identification, but that referred to documents that were not in dispute. However, in the majority of cases, whenever we proposed certain things for identification, they were rejected because the witness questioned about these documents knew nothing about them; therefore, I cannot understand how can this witness confirm the authenticity of these documents? In what way can he do that? I would understand if the witness explained anything on the map about what happened there. He didn't say anything about when this operation, Lukavica 95, took place in order for us to establish a correlation between that and air bombs. First, he has to tell us when this operation took place. You know that the indictment says that the first air bomb was used sometime in May or April. I don't know exactly. So we did not get any explanation as to what operations were involved and in which operations these air bombs you were used. At any rate, these document cannot be tendered through this witness even for identification. Of course, it is going to be up to the Trial Chamber to decide that, and I believe and I hope that the Prosecution can bring the witness through whom these documents can be tendered. In addition to that, this legend, first of all, it's not a characteristic one. It has to be signed in terms of the information contained therein. It does not contain any signature and any verification of the information contained in the boxes. It could have been put there at any time. So the legend also has to have a signature, much more so than the signature of the Dragomir Milosevic that is on the map. At any rate, the decision, Lukavica 95, has to have a link established with relevant documents. All these documents dated the 8th, the 10th, and the 12th only say "we have launchers in our possession," nothing else. Hence, I don't see in what way and how can these documents be admitted through this witness. This is my objection, and I think these are crucial matters; however, this is going to be up to the Trial Chamber to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Counsel for the Defence has addressed the issue of the map, but I don't believe the map is at issue here. That has already been admitted; and if there was a clear foundation for it from the witness for the admission of the map, I don't think there is any dispute about the admissibility of the map and the legend. My understanding was that this respect to four documents that were discussed later. And there I think our principle argument is that, number one, the appearance of authenticity, but, secondly there was no objection, and they were admitted into evidence with no objection from the Defence. And now we're having a kind of re-do, where the Defence is raising objections when it had not been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber's ruling in accordance with the practice that we have followed is that the documents 508, 509, and 510 will be marked for identification; and then I believe there are two other documents in respect of which you may want to make some application. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I've discussed the matter with Mr. Whiting, and I will move to the last question in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, does this mean that you will not seek admission of the response from Commander Radojicic and Colonel Josipovic from the 3rd Brigade as to how many air bomb launchers they were in possession of? It's fine with us; just so we know where you're heading.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will ask one question of the witness, with Your Honour's permission, with respect to the Josipovic document, dated 14 June 1995, ter number 02432. If I could ask Mr. Registrar for that document to be brought up on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, who, to your knowledge, was Colonel Dragan Josipovic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, for a long time, he was commander of one of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And was -- a second question then from that. What areas fell in the responsibility of his brigade, are you aware?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was always the commander of one brigade, all the time, or whether he changed. I cannot be more specific now. I cannot say exactly what the area of responsibility of his brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, having heard the witness' answer I -- and his familiarity with this last, I would ask for the last two documents, the Josipovic document bearing the number 02432, and it's Ilidza Brigade Radojicic document bearing the number 02428, be marked as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this case, what is being insisted upon is to have them admitted into evidence straight away. I don't see what this witness did confirm in relation to these documents and what he can confirm at all. He cannot say anything about their authenticity or how they were written or who wrote them, except for what he can read what it says on the documents themselves. About these documents, he knows absolutely nothing. I was many times in a position during these proceedings that the Defence could not have certain documents admit the because there was not sufficient material provided by the person who could have identified the document in some sense. I don't know what else I can say, but I'm opposed to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll mark them for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 02428 will be marked for identification as P511, and 65 ter number 02432 will be marked for identification as P512.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, I have one last question for you. Before August 1994 and after August 1994, until the end of the war, was there any noticeable change in the safety and security situation for the civilians in Sarajevo, as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't feel it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That concludes the examination-in-chief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm Defence counsel for General Dragomir Milosevic; and in relation to your statements, I will have to confine myself to a very limited scope, unless I have some time left later. Primary, I will deal with questions that have to do with documents, for the most part, documents that you signed while you were in command. And I will always insist on us talking about the time between the 10th of August, 1994 until the 21st of November, 1995. That is the time during which General Milosevic was commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. This is why I would like to ask that we first show on the monitor Prosecution Exhibit P42 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Repeat the number. Exhibit 42 ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P492, Prosecution Exhibit. That is dated the 23rd and 22nd of October and the 31st of October. Yes, the year is 2001, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see on this first page -- or from this first page, this is your statement Mr. Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would just like for to us deal with paragraph on page 2. In the English version, it's also on page 2, the fourth paragraph. You see how it starts: "When hostilities began in Ljubljana, our army barracks were surrounded by the territorial of Slovenia," and then you talk about some attempts that were made by the JNA and by Sipcic; and then you say: "When the Slovenian Territorial Defence cut off the water and electricity supply, Sipcic threatened to shell the entire centre of the city." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, that is correct was not done. No one shot at anyone from the barracks where you were, right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: There wasn't any significant combat. I cannot guarantee anything in terms of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the Yugoslav People's Army, precisely because of that because young soldiers were being killed in barracks, quickly withdrew from Slovenia. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And can you confirm that in Slovenia, the Territorial Defence had killed about 50 soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I know that there were soldiers killed but I cannot give you the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. When the JNA crossed over to Croatia, you were still in the Yugoslav People's Army -- or rather in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I arrived in Bosnia, but I was in the Yugoslav People's Army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But while the army was withdrawing through Croatia, you were still in the army?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was taking a unit from Ljubljana to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. The barracks in Croatia, when you were withdrawing, were they surrounded and were they fired at?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you left the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you immediately joined the Patriotic League or the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Could you separate the Patriotic League from the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. At the moment, since the state was functioning, sort of, it was a paramilitary unity then, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: That's what you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I have just heard that the transcript does to the reflect that the witness became a member of the Patriotic League. Could that please be entered in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: But it is in the transcript, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, later. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. But from what I see on the transcript, he asked -- the witness asked Mr. Tapuskovic to separate the Patriotic League from the Green Berets, and then a further question was asked. And the witness did not confirm his membership in either of those organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let's ask him. Were you a member of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did work according to tasks given to me by the political top echelons of Sarajevo, and it can be called work of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And were you a member of the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us focus for a moment on this problem. Now, when the Yugoslav People's Army arrived in Sarajevo, at one point in time were the barracks there in Sarajevo too surrounded by members of the territorial and by members of the Patriotic League that you were a member of? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of August, 1991, I brought my battalion to the barracks in Zenica in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is where I stayed for all of two months. During that period of time, that barracks was not touched in any way by anyone. On the 20th of October, I moved to the Husinjska Buna barracks in Tuzla, and that is where I stayed until the enter of 1991. I claim with full responsibility that no one touched those barracks, too, and no one tried to touch them in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. But we can say at any rate that in 1991, in January, right, you were already the leader of a battalion of the Patriotic League, right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: You mean 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, 1992.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1992, up until the war, I was registered as the coordinator of the Patriotic League for the area of north-west Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: North-east Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These were armed units?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: These were people without units, up until somewhere in February or March. People with their own weapons depending on who had what type of weapons, hunting weapons, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The war started in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Officially, on the 6th of April, 1992, in terms of legal norms, but it started a lot earlier on the 1st of April, in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But wasn't it Sjekovac that came first, the massacre of 30 Serbs, nearby in Bosanski Novi in March? You don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Indeed, this is the first time I hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we now move on to page 3. I beg your pardon. I do apologise. Really, I have just received a suggestion from the accused. I said Bosanski Novi, but Sjekovac is near Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: It doesn't really mean anything it me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now we're dealing with page 3. And in the English version it is the fifth paragraph on page 3, and the B/C/S version is paragraph 3 from the bottom. You say here: "When leaving the JNA, I joined the Patriotic League of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The idea for the league had originated from gathering of several hundreds politicians and SDA members led by President Izetbegovic in June 1991. The idea was to organise the population to defend itself in case of attack." Is it correct that these military units in the form of the Patriotic League started functioning as far back as June 1991? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Next paragraph: "When I left the JNA, I became the commander of the Patriotic League for north-east Bosnia. The task of the preparing the population was not simply in obtaining weapons." But that's it? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Inter alia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you made an effort to arm the people, the population, even then before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Because I was an officer of the JNA until that point in time, and I saw what it was that the Yugoslav People's Army was preparing and that is why I had to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that the barracks in Slovenia were surrounded, and I'm not going to back to had an it was that you said or to what happened in Croatia in May and late May in particular. Did the Patriotic League surround even hospitals and barracks in Sarajevo, and you also participated in that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Look, I am really trying to be as brief as possible in terms of the answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There are two questions in that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There are two questions in that, Your Honour, and perhaps the witness will be entitled to answer one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And the first question was...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My submission, Your Honour, is that the first question would be did the Patriotic League surround hospitals and barracks in Sarajevo. The second question would be whether or not the witness took part in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm grateful for that. Answer the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Patriotic League did not surround hospitals and barracks. During that period of time, I could not have been there. I could not have participated because I was in prison in Serbia in Sremska Mitrovica near Belgrade. I had been taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when were you taken prisoner, in what military action? Because obviously you took part in military action. How was it that you were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: If you think that this is it action, to come to attend a meeting with the head of the municipality of Zivinice near Tuzla, also in Focakovic, then that is your view. I was taken prisoner in that office, in the office of the head of the municipality of Zivinice, because in conjunction with officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, from the military air field of Dubrava near Tuzla, there was an agreement. They betrayed me, and I was handed over to the JNA; then I was taken by helicopter to Belgrade and then to prisoner in Sremska Mitrovica, and I was sentenced to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What were these proceedings, and after all you were not executed, the death sentence was not carried out?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The death sentence was not carried out only thanks to God All Mighty, and the fact that Alija Izetbegovic was detained at the airport in May 1992. So when he was exchange in Sarajevo with Kukanjac, General Kukanjac, the commander of the 2nd Military District, then the territorial defence in Sarajevo took prisoner about 200 JNA officers. So in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're speaking too fast. The interpreter is having difficult keeping up with you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The court reporters cannot record everything that is being said at this speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was exchanged for General Kukanjac the commander of the 2nd Military District of the JNA in Sarajevo, then the members of the territorial defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina took prisoner in Sarajevo about 200 military officers of the JNA. In order to get those officers back, and especially one of the key officers, Suput, and yet another one, Bijalosovic, who were the first assistants of General Aca Vasiljevic, I managed to be set free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Will you tell us more about these proceedings as a result of which you were sentenced to death. What proceedings were these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't similar to this, but there were also three presiding persons, like the three of you sitting now. Three colonels in a separate building in a separate room in the prison in Sremska Mitrovica. It was that court that was interrogating me for 13 days at the end, quite literally. There are records of that. I'm sure that Mr. Tapuskovic can get them from Belgrade. He can; I cannot. When they asked me after that, "You're bound to be sentenced to death." That's what they said to me. "Finally, let us ask you, how you would like to be executed," and my answer was, "I would kindly request that only a bullet be used and nothing else."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you charged with any offences; and if so, what were the offences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The basic point in the indictment was treason to the Yugoslav People's Army and violation of the constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, or rather, desertion from the Yugoslav People's Army. I had deserted from the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. Sorry. Did you have a lawyer to defend you in the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You did not mention the most important thing of all, that was referred to there was primarily this armed rebellion because the state was still in existence, and you were a member of the Patriotic League, as an illegal, illegitimate paramilitary formation. Is that what was referred to most of all?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: If you want the truth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that my friend rephrase the question, because in my submission it's not for counsel on either side to testify as to the nature of any organisation. Mr. Tapuskovic in asking the question to the witness has told the witness that the Patriotic League was an illegal, illegitimate paramilitary formation, and I would ask the question be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why? Why can't he put it to the witness that that was the nature of the organisation? He needs to put his case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He can put his case to the witness, Your Honour, but in my submission it's not for my friend to give evidence as to the nature of at organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. He is not giving evidence. He is putting it to him that that was the nature of the organisation to which he belonged, and it is for the witness to say whether that is so or not. What is your answer to the question put to you by Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave my answer to you personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't hear it. The question that was put to you was that you didn't mention the most important aspect relating to your case, which is that you were a member of the Patriotic League which was an illegal and an illegitimate paramilitary organisation. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In one of my statements, you can find this. It is written there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must answer the question that I have asked. What is your answer to the question? Don't direct me to your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I sincerely apologise. I thought that you asked me that this was omitted in the statement. It is in my statement and can I repeat my answer. Patriotic League was an informal organisation. Its objective was exclusively to achieve political mobility in the event of Bosnia-Herzegovina being attacked and subjected to aggression; the enlightenment of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know, just like everybody else, and it is also in the literature probably by your people, that in January 1992, the Patriotic League had 120.000 people under arms. Sefer Halilovic confirmed that categorically in his book?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I don't know what Sefer Halilovic claims, but I can say that in north-east Bosnia, where I was, that there were -- that the people had weapons, but more than 90 per cent of those weapons were hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me one more thing in relation to this. You complained what transpired in Slovenia and what happened in Croatia, and you said a while ago the thing about President Izetbegovic and the 2nd of May. Can you confirm that in Bosnia-Herzegovina this happened also: After the army started withdrawing from the barracks on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1992, a massacre of soldiers took place, of soldiers who were peacefully leaving the barracks in a column? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I cannot, because at the time I was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that several hundred people while withdrawing from Tuzla, or rather, several hundred soldiers were killed while they were peacefully retreating from Tuzla toward Serbia? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I know very well what this is all about. You are asking me just to say yes or no. This was a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can the witness please repeat the location?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We didn't hear the location, the place that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Brcanska Malta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I put it to you that according to reliable sources of information, this column was leaving completely peacefully; and at a very inconvenient place, the soldiers were killed? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: You are asking me about the soldiers and the barracks that I had deserted from a few months before that, so I know these things much better than you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All of a sudden you know about that. A while ago you didn't know anything about Dobrovoljacka, but you said that you were prison when this happened in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How come you know for sure now what happened?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I know what happened in Dobrovoljacka because I heard about that. I didn't see it with my own eyes. I wouldn't comment on the Tuzla incident, but you are leading me in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have exhausted this subject. Let's move to page 13 of your statement. It's page 12 in the English version, last passage. This is what you say here. That's paragraph 3 in the B/C/S version. You talk about the change of tactics, and you say as follows: "In 1994, we changed our tactics and tried to take the majority of our forces --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This is not the reference which counsel gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't get any English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The reference given by the counsel is obviously not the correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, please provide with us the correct reference; page and paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 12 in the English version, last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think it's the last paragraph under the heading, "Attempts to break out of Sarajevo," which is in the middle of page 12. Thanks to Mr. Registrar and Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We now have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What's written here, is it correct you said yes?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Because I finally realised that Sarajevo cannot be open from inside as a can. You don't open a can from inside. That is why I changed the tactics with a view to opening this can, i.e., Sarajevo, from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain whether you could have opened this can from the outside if you didn't have the tunnel that existed under the airport?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: No. Because the SRK kept Sarajevo in the can; that is, under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did this siege exist still in place because you had an opportunity to go through the tunnel. Who was under siege actually?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Nothing changed. The citizens of Sarajevo were still under siege. The tunnel was used only for military purposes and for the supply of weapons. Sarajevo was still without water, without electricity, without gas, food, and all other necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please look at page 14, and page 13 in the English version, paragraph 4, if I got it right. You say here again, but you elaborate a bit. "At the beginning of 1994, we started to counterattack and many of our forces moved out of the city, which we had concluded could not be successfully defended from within. During 1994, we regained much of the ground that we had lost during the VRS offensive, and we attempted to encircle part of the VRS forces." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In principle and generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was this particular characteristic for the period between August 1994 and the end of the conflict in November 1995? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: That was characteristic from the moment the tunnel was built, and that is the 1st of August, 1994 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Initially, the tunnel was not in the condition that it was in later?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Please don't talk about this to me. I know in which connection it was. I built it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. However, in 1994, I understand the justification with regard to food and medicine, but much more weapons passed through the tunnel and entered Sarajevo; Hundreds of thousands of tons, as Alija Izetbegovic says in his book called, "Memory."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are proceeding much too fast, both of you. The interpreter is having great difficulty keeping up with the pace, so please slow down and don't overlap. You have to wait for the interpretation to finish. I'm speaking to both of you, Mr. Tapuskovic and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question about the tunnel wasn't recorded in the transcript. I have to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The tunnel that was built under the airport made it possible in the period between August 1994 and November 1995, of course, for people to receive supplies of food and medicines; however, on most occasions, it was used for the flow of enormous quantities of weapons entering Sarajevo as a demilitarised zone? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: It was, first and foremost, used for the passage of soldiers and it's wounded. Secondly, it was used for food supplies; and, thirdly, it was used for various types of ammunition and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But it was mostly used for fresh troops to leave Sarajevo and go to the front line where attacks were launched on Ilijas, Ilidza, and further on towards Trnovo and Nisic Viseron [phoen]? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I'm just finishing a book about the Sarajevo's war tunnel, and you will soon be able to read it. In terms of time, of usage, the most time was used for providing food supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will just like to tackle two more topics relating to your statement. The next one is on page 16 of the B/C/S version, and page 15, second -- English version page 15, paragraph 2, heading "Use of mobile mortars in Sarajevo." I'm going to read it very slowly to you. "Unauthorized use of mobile mortars in Sarajevo caused a great deal of trouble for me and for the 1st Corps," and further on, "They were never able to locate such mortar, not even the military police. I was never able to clearly establish their ownership or even their existence. "Even today I do not know who controlled or commanded these weapons. It was certainly not the policy of the corps to use such weapons in Sarajevo in that manner. I asked UNPROFOR to intervene directly in this matter." Please, is this correct? Is this true that you never knew who it was?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In retrospect, I'm deeply convinced that this was a fabricated term by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and promoted as such through UNPROFOR, in order to provide them with an alibi for all their inhumane treatment of the city, and what is written in the report is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Witness, you said in the first sentence that it was an unauthorised use of mobile mortars. You knew at the time that these mortars were being used. This is what you said in your first sentence? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: This is ridiculous. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also had terrorists organisations in Sarajevo such as Seva that was involved in and committing acts contrary to the will of your corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I would advise you not to use the word "terrorist." This is your opinion. This unit did exist, but it was not a terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me move quickly to another two topics. B/C/S version page 15, English version page 14, paragraph 4, so I have to go back a little. Here you say that you had to remove Fikret Prevljak, who was the commander of the 12th Division in Sarajevo - that's the one that existed and operated in Sarajevo and from Sarajevo - and also Ismet Hadzic; is this true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: What is your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You write here that you removed these two gentlemen. Why?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Because of indiscipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Hadn't they, during the conflict and particularly recently, been accused or suspected of killing Serbs and Muslims and everybody else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just one moment. Let's hear the answer first to your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know nothing about anyone being suspected of this kind of acts that this gentleman is referring to, that involved Fikret Prevljak and Brigadier Hadzic. They are all living as free people in Sarajevo, and I know of no indictment being issued against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You also had serious disagreement and conflict with the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigade and their commanders. Is it true that you settled your scores in a way with them, precisely because they were suspected of numerous killings of Croats and Muslims at the beginning of war, even in their thousands? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Before Ms. Edgerton says that you're asking two questions, let us separate them. Did you have serious disagreement with the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigade and their commanders? What is the answer to that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You did. And then is it true that you settled your scores with them because they were suspected of numerous killings of Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for part of the answer, yes. As for another part of the answer, no. As for this, yes. Yes, I did settle my scores with them. As for one brigade commander and a number of his officers, we did away with them. We liquidated them. And an another brigade commander and some 300 officers almost and soldiers, we put them into prison. Therefore, before the cantonal court in Sarajevo, I think there are still ongoing proceedings. Why they were the way they were and why I settled this with them in this way is primarily due to a lack of discipline; and, secondly, because they committed violations against the non-Bosniak population in very small numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to put to you some documents. I have quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please put Defence exhibit D106 on the monitor. There is a translation there, too, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see the document? It says how many people the 1st Corps had in the beginning of August 1994. Can you confirm on the basis of this document that was signed by Halilagic, the person in charge, that then the 1st Corps had 62.899 persons or members.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I know that in 1993, the 1st Corps was the one with the largest number of soldiers. 63.000, this is a bit less. So I confirm this if this is an official document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Honourable Witness, I got this document in the archives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was confirmed by the appropriate official of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Then there is no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we say that the 1st Corps consisted of three division: The 12th, 14th, 16th, respectively?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that two corps, the 14th and 16th, were outside Sarajevo, and the 12th was in Sarajevo in its entirety? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: You're referring to divisions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Divisions.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then in Sarajevo there were certainly 40.000 members of this 12th Division?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The figure ranged from 30 to 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, can we say that in addition to the divisions and brigades, there were a few independent manoeuvring brigades: The 141st, 43rd, and 46th?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that there was engineering, military police, artillery --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is meant by "independent manoeuvreing brigades"? Let mow ask the witness because he did answer yes. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout the war, I had brigades, many of them that were static and that held the defence line, and their number ranged from three to 5.000 soldiers. At the end of 1994 and beginning of 1995, I decided to single out from these units some soldiers and to have a few small manoeuvreing brigades that would have up to 1.000 soldiers. They would not be on the defence line only. They would not be stuck to that line, but they could go to wherever a breakthrough was attempted and also wherever they could be needed for offensive activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will stop now and resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of March, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
